\chapter{More Short Replies}
\label{ch:ka-more-replies}
\hlchaptermodality{58}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer an offer in Kannada five ways, from a little to no thank you.}

Complete KA-C58-thats-all and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[svalpa]{\kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ} (svalpa) — a little, a bit}

\label{lesson:KA-C58-a-little}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{bhuja} mean, and what did \emph{mūḷe} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ}} (\emph{svalpa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a little, a bit\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit, and it comes apart cleanly: \emph{su-}, \textquotedblleft{}well, nicely\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{alpa}, \textquotedblleft{}small\textquotedblright{}. Nicely small. The same \emph{su-} that opens the good-morning word you already have.

But the useful thing about \kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ} is not its size. It is what it does to whatever follows it. Ask for something flat and you are instructing; put \kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ} in front and you are asking. \kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ} \kn{ನೀರು} \kn{ಕೊಡಿ} leaves the other person room to move in a way that \kn{ನೀರು} \kn{ಕೊಡಿ} does not.

The word measures a quantity in the dictionary and a manner in the mouth. English does the same thing with \textquotedblleft{}just\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}a bit\textquotedblright{}, and neither of those measures much any more either.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word that softens the next one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{svalpa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nīru koḍi}, then \emph{svalpa nīru koḍi}, and hear how much softer the second one is
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a little, a bit\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[heccu]{\kn{ಹೆಚ್ಚು} (heccu) — more, a lot}

\label{lesson:KA-C58-more}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{svalpa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಹೆಚ್ಚು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಹೆಚ್ಚು}} (\emph{heccu}) — \textquotedblleft{}more, a lot\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, and the opening \emph{h} puts it in the same layer as \kn{ಹಣ್ಣು} and \kn{ಹಳ್ಳಿ}. The borrowed word softened your request; this one is Kannada's own, and it does the opposite job.

\kn{ಹೆಚ್ಚು} is both \textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}much\textquotedblright{}. It answers a question about quantity all by itself, and it goes in front of whatever it is measuring: \kn{ಹೆಚ್ಚು} \kn{ಹಣ್ಣು}, more fruit. It is also the word for a comparison, so \kn{ಹೆಚ್ಚು} is how a Kannada speaker says one thing outweighs another without needing a separate word for \textquotedblleft{}than\textquotedblright{}.

Held against \kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ} it gives you a scale you can answer with. \kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ} when a little will do; \kn{ಹೆಚ್ಚು} when it will not.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and they point in opposite directions.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{heccu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{svalpa hālu}, then \emph{heccu hālu}, and hear the amount change in front
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಹೆಚ್ಚು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}more, a lot\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kaḍime]{\kn{ಕಡಿಮೆ} (kaḍime) — less, fewer}

\label{lesson:KA-C58-less}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{heccu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಕಡಿಮೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಕಡಿಮೆ}} (\emph{kaḍime}) — \textquotedblleft{}less, fewer\textquotedblright{}.

Underneath sits \kn{ಕಡಿ} (\emph{kaḍi}), to cut, to reduce. \kn{ಕಡಿಮೆ} is the cut-down amount — a quantity named for the act that produced it, which is the same move Kannada made with the fruit-word, where the ripening gave the ripe thing its name.

\kn{ಹೆಚ್ಚು} and \kn{ಕಡಿಮೆ} travel together as a pair, and the pair has its own life. \kn{ಹೆಚ್ಚು} \kn{ಕಡಿಮೆ}, said as one phrase, means \textquotedblleft{}more or less, roughly\textquotedblright{} — two opposites put side by side to make a hedge. English builds \textquotedblleft{}more or less\textquotedblright{} out of exactly the same two pieces, and Kannada leaves out the \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}.

That is three of the five now, and none of them names a thing. This chapter is about the words that adjust everything else.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and two of them make a phrase together.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kaḍime}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{heccu kaḍime}, and say what the pair means when it travels as one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಕಡಿಮೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}less, fewer\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bēḍa]{\kn{ಬೇಡ} (bēḍa) — no thank you, I don't want it}

\label{lesson:KA-C58-no-thanks}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kaḍime} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬೇಡ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಬೇಡ}} (\emph{bēḍa}) — \textquotedblleft{}no thank you, I don't want it\textquotedblright{}.

This is the refusal a guest actually needs, and it is not the \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} you learned on the first page. \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} denies that something exists or is so. \kn{ಬೇಡ} declines it.

It is the negative twin of \kn{ಬೇಕು} (\emph{bēku}), \textquotedblleft{}wanted, needed\textquotedblright{} — the word that turns up in the sort of sentence Kannada builds with nothing doing at all. \kn{ಬೇಕು} and \kn{ಬೇಡ} answer the same question in opposite directions, and neither of them bothers to name who is doing the wanting. The offer is made, and one word settles it.

At a Kannada table you will be offered more food several times after you are finished. \kn{ಬೇಡ}, said once and pleasantly, is the whole of the reply. Adding \kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ} in front turns it into \textquotedblleft{}just a little\textquotedblright{}, which is the answer that gets you served anyway.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one is the polite way out.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bēḍa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bēḍa}, then \emph{illa}, and say which one refuses and which one denies
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಬೇಡ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}no thank you, I don't want it\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aṣṭē]{\kn{ಅಷ್ಟೇ} (aṣṭē) — that's all, just that}

\label{lesson:KA-C58-thats-all}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bēḍa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಅಷ್ಟೇ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಅಷ್ಟೇ}} (\emph{aṣṭē}) — \textquotedblleft{}that's all, just that\textquotedblright{}.

Two pieces. \kn{ಅಷ್ಟು} (\emph{aṣṭu}) is \textquotedblleft{}that much\textquotedblright{}, and it belongs to the pointing family you already have — the \emph{a-} of \kn{ಅದು} and \kn{ಅಲ್ಲಿ}, the one that means away from the speaker. Then the long \emph{-ē} on the end, which Kannada hangs on a word to mean \textquotedblleft{}and nothing besides\textquotedblright{}.

So \kn{ಅಷ್ಟೇ} is \textquotedblleft{}that much, and no more\textquotedblright{}. It closes a list, ends an order, and stops a question. Asked what else you would like: \kn{ಅಷ್ಟೇ}.

That closing \emph{-ē} is worth keeping. Put it on almost anything and you get \textquotedblleft{}only that one\textquotedblright{}: \kn{ಇಲ್ಲಿಯೇ}, right here and nowhere else. One small sound doing the work English needs a whole separate word for.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \kn{ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ}, \kn{ಹೆಚ್ಚು}, \kn{ಕಡಿಮೆ}, \kn{ಬೇಡ}, \kn{ಅಷ್ಟೇ}. You can answer an offer five ways.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{aṣṭē}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{aṣṭē}, as though closing a list
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಅಷ್ಟೇ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}that's all, just that\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
